newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota net seen soaring on weaker yen.
newsitem.headline: Toyota net seen soaring on weaker yen.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp, the world's Number Two carmaker, cruised to impressive profits in the first half of the business year, powered by the weaker yen and effective cost-cutting, analysts say.

Toyota, Japan's biggest carmaker, is likely to have easily exceeded its own earnings target for the period to the end of September and will post profits of around 250 billion yen ($2.23 billion), car industry analysts say.

The profits bonanza was achieved through cuts in production costs, by using the same parts in several models, as well as a windfall from the weaker yen. Toyota will announce its half-year earnings on November 8 along with rivals such as Nissan, which is also expected to see profits rise.

Toyota's expected 250 billion yen ($2.23 billion) in parent current profit in the first six months of this fiscal year would be 40 billion yen ($357 million) more than its own forecast made in May, said Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura. Toyota made an actual 68.06 billion yen ($607 million) in the first half of fiscal 1995/96. Current profit is pre-tax and includes non-operating activities such as profits or losses on the sale of shareholdings.
Toyota had assumed an average exchange rate of 100 yen to the dollar in this business year, against 96 a year earlier.

The value of the dollar now stands at around 112 yen. A decline of one yen against the dollar translates into at least another 10 billion yen ($89.2 million) of profit a year for Toyota, as a weaker yen makes Japanese exports more competitive overseas.
Analysts said the exact size of Toyota's profit would depend on how much money it chose to plough back into advertising and incentives to dealers.

Noriyuki Matsushima, a senior analyst at Nikko Research, said Toyota's current profit in the year to March 1997 would be around 550 billion yen ($4.91 billion), mainly because of the weaker yen. In May, Toyota forecast a parent current profit of 480 billion yen ($4.28 billion) in 1996/97 against an actual 340.73 billion yen ($3.04 billion) a year earlier.

Sugiura said Toyota's profit for the year may reach 600 billion yen ($5.35 billion) in the current yen/dollar situation, compared with a previous Nomura Research forecast of 530 billion yen ($4.73 billion).
Kankaku Research senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi said the figure would exceed 500 billion yen ($4.46 billion) if the exchange rate remained at around the current level.

Toyota's domestic vehicle production rose 6.2 percent from a year earlier to 1.62 million units in the April to September period. Its vehicle exports rose 17.1 percent to 664,145 in the same period, while its domestic sales stood at 957,526, little changed from the year-earlier period.

Toyota's vehicle production would continue to rise because of the current increase in its exports, helped by the weaker yen, Matsushima said. Its domestic sales were also expected to grow when it launched new models, he said. Increased production volume would result in bigger cost savings, the analysts said.
Toyota has launched a total of 10 models in Japan since January and will launch at least one more by December.

On Wednesday, Kazushi Iwatsuki, a Toyota director in charge of vehicle sales, said Toyota would be able to reach a 40 percent share of the domestic market in calendar 1996 because of strong demand for its new models. Its share in the January-September period stood at 38.4 percent, down 0.8 percentage point from the same period a year ago.
